narrative:
The model determined that you have a 50% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability met the school's threshold for risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. While the average student who was accepted ranked in the top 5.8 decile by their third year, you placed in the third decile, signaling a noticeable drop in performance that the model interpreted as a warning sign for bar exam success.

Your choice to attend law school part-time was the second most important factor. This pulled the prediction in the opposite direction, slightly increasing the chance you would pass. However, because only 7% of accepted students plan to study part-time, the model viewed this as an uncommon path that could not fully offset other risks.

Your first-year class ranking came third. At the sixth decile, it matched the average of accepted students and therefore provided a modest positive influence toward passing, but it was not strong enough to overcome the concerns raised by your later academic performance.

Taken together, the model saw your declining grades in law school as the dominant signal. To strengthen future applications, focus on improving your academic trajectory if possible, consider full-time study, and retake the LSAT to raise your score closer to the 37-point average of successful applicants. These steps would directly address the factors that led to this outcome.
